title: Early records, listening to Louis Armstrong, learning Confessin'
summary: He recalls no local band recording early, admired Louis Armstrong on radio and records, and learned Confessin' from Edmund Walsh.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: He did a lot of, but he tape a lot of bands. What was the first band that you remember making any records from around here? Could you remember any of the bands? My band. Not my band, but with Millie Barnes and them. I don't mean the first- I don't mean the first record you made, I mean do you remember anybody else's band making records? Can you remember one?
No, no, I don't remember nobody else making no records. And them, I tell you, them did, you see them did, they had all these things they got, no.
Did you ever used to listen to any jazz records when you first had your band?

Did you ever listen to any jazz records? Yeah. Listen to what you call it, Lister Armstrong. See, Lister Armstrong left for me and went to Chicago, played with what you call it. In them days people even had radio. Like you had radio, people would come on, you see, you'd come on at a certain time of the evening, everybody would run to them people out and listen to that, you know what I mean? Like you wouldn't have no radio for a couple of, you know what I mean? You'd come on at a certain time in the evening, you know. So I used to listen to him. Well I always did like his playing. I liked Lister Armstrong playing before all the trumpet players. I liked it, you see. But the plenty of people would say, well why you don't play like this? I said no, I said play my own style. I said well I just like his style, I like his playing. I mean I'll go to the club, because I know he can play, you know what I mean? So no, I used to listen to that record. We used to take the record and line off them, you know what I mean? Line the songs off them.
Yeah. What are Lister Armstrong's records you mean?
Sure. And did you know that tune, Confessing, from the Lister record? What? Confessing, did you know that from Lister's record?

I don't believe, no. No, I confess, no. I learned from somebody. I mean Walsh, Edmund Walsh, and start playing that. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Edmund Walsh, yeah. He started playing it. Yeah, yeah. He started playing it. Yeah, Walsh. He used to sing it, you know. Yeah, you learned it from him. But I'll tell you what, after we had the band up and everything, and I played at the Monroe Rouge, you see what? We was playing, Larkport, racing, Larkport, Gold Medal, all the way down to Grand Island, Tibido, Bomo, Baton Rouge, all the way up, you know what I mean? So we, you see when I, then I started, this man started running dance at the Monroe Rouge during the time of the war. Well we was playing it racing, we was playing racing on Saturday. And what you call them had a job. Wilford Buck Island had a job on Leponia, what you call it. By the river? Yeah, in Chapitula. Playing for this boy had a bar, you see, and a nice place you know. Well they had been playing it so long, so this guy asked me, say kid, say you don't want a job? He said man we got tired playing. So we took this job, you know, where we used to play. We played Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. And Saturday we'd go to racing, you see. So all right. Then right after that the war broke out, see. So now this man, you'll expect, we were going to play from before, you know. So during the time of the war it was kind of hard to get lumber, because he wanted to build a dance hall. He went all over, you know, buying lumber, you know, used lumber and everything. So we played over there, you know, chopping through the street. So Joe James pulled Joe there and there and going, Joe lived up there, he was living up there. He asked Joe, he told Joe, he said I need a band. He said I want a good sized band, a big band. You know what I mean? Joe said, yeah we'll give you a big band. So sure enough. So what we did, we started playing for him. Who was in the band at that time?
